analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by payroll premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat and a Republican with 5 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let workers take the leave they already have a right to under the Family and Medical Leave Act and get paid for it — up to 8 weeks, replacing a larger share of wages for lower earners (100% for workers earning under $20,000, tapering to 40% for high earners). Employers and employees would each pay a 0.2% payroll premium into a federal trust fund; small employers with fewer than 50 workers would be exempt unless they chose to join, and employers with equivalent private plans could opt out. A separate program would cover federal employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need leave for a new baby, adoption, a serious illness of their own, or to care for a child, spouse, or parent but cannot afford unpaid time off — the bill's findings cite a Labor Department survey finding 78% of employees who need FMLA leave but don't take it skip it because they can't afford it [S3]. Lower-wage workers benefit most, since their wages would be fully or mostly replaced [S3]. Federal employees would get the same benefits through a civil service program [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who can't afford unpaid leave

how_it_helps.text: Provides up to 8 workweeks of paid leave per year for birth, adoption, foster care placement, a serious health condition, or caring for a child, spouse, or parent [S2].
Replaces 100% of daily earnings for workers earning $20,000 or less, with progressively smaller shares for higher earners, and indexes the income brackets over time [S3].
Finances benefits through a dedicated trust fund fed by a 0.2% payroll premium on employees and a matching 0.2% premium on employers, with small employers exempt unless they opt in [S3].
Prohibits employers from interfering with leave rights or retaliating against workers who use them, with civil damages, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees for violations [S3].
Extends the same paid-leave benefit to covered federal agency employees through a separate civil service program [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and employees would each pay a 0.2% payroll premium, and self-employed individuals who opt in would pay 0.2% of self-employment income. Employers with fewer than 50 employees would pay nothing unless they elect to participate, and any employer whose own plan is certified as equivalent or better would be exempt [S3]. Employers would front the benefit payments to workers and be reimbursed from the trust fund [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and employees via payroll premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new mandatory payroll tax of 0.2% on every employee and 0.2% on every employer nationwide, a permanent cost on businesses and workers even for those who never take leave [S3].
Employers must pay leave benefits to workers upfront and wait for reimbursement from the fund, which creates cash-flow and administrative burdens, especially for smaller covered employers [S3].

If the trust fund runs short, the managing trustee publishes a notice of insufficient funds and employers are no longer required to pay leave benefits until the fund is replenished — meaning the benefit could be suspended when funding falls behind [S3].

Higher earners receive much less wage replacement — above $97,000 the benefit is capped at 40% of a $97,000 earner's daily wages — so the program is least valuable to those with the least flexibility to take unpaid time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real and concentrated on those least able to absorb unpaid leave, and the cost is spread thinly (a 0.2% payroll premium on both sides) across all covered employers and employees rather than concentrated on one industry. The design has genuine flaws: employers front the money and wait for reimbursement, and an insolvency clause lets employers stop paying benefits if the fund is short. The benefits-for-cost tradeoff is favorable to working people overall, which is precisely why its cost drew opposition from employer groups.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2007, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on June 21, 2007, joined by Senator Ted Stevens, a Republican, making it bipartisan at introduction [S3].
Five senators cosponsored the bill — four Democrats and one Republican [S4].
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S5].
The Finance Committee never took up the bill, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the 0.2% payroll premium, and any groups opposed to a new federal paid-leave entitlement, are better off because the bill never advanced; workers who needed paid leave gained nothing from its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid the premium

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor the day it was introduced

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Joined Dodd as the bill's co-introducer, making it bipartisan at introduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended

against.what_they_did: Aside from one cosponsor, did not advance the bill, and no Senate Republican leader moved it toward the floor

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — Dodd, a Democrat, and Stevens, a Republican, introduced it together, and its 5 cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of a floor fight was never tested.

industries.note: Employers would pay a 0.2% payroll premium and front leave payments to workers before reimbursement from the trust fund. The cost is broad-based rather than concentrated in one industry, and small employers under 50 workers were exempt.

The bill requires that employer voluntary plans provide insurance issued by an approved admitted disability insurer or equivalent self-insurance, creating a private-market role for insurers in paid-leave coverage. Insurers would profit from this channel while workers receive benefits through it.
